slides.title: Title
slides.notes: Open by framing the chapter as the point where manifold theory and algebraic structure lock together. The audience should hear that every visual in the lecture is a dictionary entry: a global group operation, a local tangent object, and a theorem explaining when the two determine each other.

slides.title: Lie Group Definition
slides.notes: Use this slide to separate the algebraic and geometric requirements. A topological or abstract group is not enough; the group operations must respect the smooth structure. Emphasize that the single smooth map to ab inverse efficiently contains both multiplication and inversion.

slides.title: Left Invariant Algebra
slides.notes: The important move is that a Lie group has enough translation symmetry to make tangent data global. A left invariant vector field is completely determined by its value at the identity, and the bracket of such fields stays left invariant, giving the tangent space its algebra structure.

slides.title: Matrix Group Lab
slides.notes: This slide connects the abstract definition to a checkable laboratory. For SO(2), the group is cut out by equations inside matrix space. Differentiating the equations at the identity gives the skew-symmetric generator, and the notebook verifies that the displayed rotations satisfy the constraints numerically.

slides.title: Exponential Map
slides.notes: Emphasize that exponential is not merely a formula for matrices. It is defined by the universal property of one-parameter subgroups. In SO(2), the real line of angles maps onto a periodic group, which exposes the difference between local tangent data and global topology.

slides.title: Homomorphisms Differentiate
slides.notes: Present this as the first direction of the global-local dictionary. A smooth group homomorphism necessarily respects the infinitesimal algebra. The proof is not a computation in coordinates; it uses the fact that the homomorphism intertwines left translations and therefore carries left invariant fields to left invariant fields.

slides.title: Integrating Algebra Maps
slides.notes: This is a good place to slow down and name the hypotheses. Connectedness gives uniqueness because a homomorphism is generated from any neighborhood of the identity. Simple connectivity gives existence by letting the integral graph of a differential ideal project without monodromy obstruction.

slides.title: Subgroups From Subalgebras
slides.notes: Tie this theorem back to Chapter 1 and Chapter 2 tools. The subalgebra is converted into a distribution by left translation, and Frobenius supplies an integral manifold. The group structure of the leaf is not automatic from Frobenius alone; it follows from left invariance and maximality.

slides.title: Coverings
slides.notes: Use the line over the circle as the mental model for this part of the chapter. The derivative can be an isomorphism while the global map still wraps several times. Covering groups repair that mismatch by replacing the source with a simply connected Lie group upstairs.

slides.title: Classical Matrix Groups
slides.notes: This slide should feel computational. The classical groups are not just examples; they are test cases showing how equations on matrices linearize to Lie algebra conditions and then exponentiate back to nearby group elements. The trace, orthogonality, and unitary conditions become tangent algebra constraints.

slides.title: Lie Bracket
slides.notes: Use the triangular loop to explain what the bracket detects. If the X flow and Y flow commuted perfectly, the small loop would close without first-order defect. In the matrix laboratory, the commutator makes that defect exact and keeps the result inside trace-zero matrices.

slides.title: Adjoint Representation
slides.notes: The adjoint representation is the internal symmetry of the Lie algebra produced by the group itself. The class should see conjugation as a global group operation that fixes the identity, then differentiation turns it into a linear algebra automorphism preserving brackets and detecting the center.

slides.title: Closed Subgroup Theorem
slides.notes: Stress that this is one of the chapter's strongest structural results. A subgroup is initially only an algebraic subset with the relative topology. Closedness supplies enough compactness and limit control for exponential coordinates to identify a tangent subspace and build the smooth subgroup structure.

slides.title: Homogeneous Manifolds
slides.notes: This slide ties together closed subgroups and group actions. The quotient is smooth because closed subgroups have the right embedded structure. Conversely, a transitive action turns the manifold into a quotient by the stabilizer, so homogeneous spaces are the geometric form of orbit-stabilizer reasoning.

slides.title: Reading Protocol
slides.notes: This slide converts the chapter into a workflow students can reuse. In a matrix example, they should first locate the defining equations, differentiate them, compute the bracket, exponentiate tangent directions, and then decide what the global topology and subgroup hypotheses allow them to conclude.

slides.title: Hypotheses
slides.notes: Use this warning slide to prevent overgeneralization. Students often remember the slogan that Lie groups are determined by Lie algebras, but the chapter is careful about connectedness, simple connectivity, closedness, and normality. Each hypothesis pays for a specific global conclusion.

slides.title: Recap
slides.notes: Close by returning to the dictionary motif from the title slide. The chapter is not a list of unrelated theorems; it is a system for moving between smooth symmetry, tangent algebra, exponentials, covering topology, subgroup structure, and homogeneous quotient geometry with exactly stated hypotheses.
